title: The river was supposed to be a grave.
paragraphs: The river was supposed to be a grave.
That was Pharaoh’s plan.

A decree had gone out across Egypt:
Every Hebrew baby boy must die.
Thrown into the Nile. Erased before he could even learn his own name.
Imagine the terror of that moment in history.

Every cry of a newborn boy could become a death sentence.
Every mother lived with the sound of soldiers in the distance.
Every family waited for the knock that might steal their child.

And in the middle of that darkness…
one woman refused to surrender to fear.
Her name was Jochebed.

She looked at her baby boy and saw something others might have missed. Scripture says she saw that he was beautiful (Exodus 2:2). But this was not merely about appearance. In faith, she recognized something precious—something worth risking everything to protect.
So she hid him.

Day after day.
Night after night.
Listening for footsteps.
Holding her breath whenever the baby cried.
Three months.

Three months of courage.
Three months of whispered prayers.
Three months of fighting a system designed to destroy him.
But eventually, hiding was no longer possible.
And here is where the story becomes unbearable.
Because faith sometimes leads you to a moment where you must release what you love most.

Jochebed made a small basket out of papyrus reeds.
She sealed it with tar and pitch so the water could not seep in.
The Hebrew word used here is “tevah.”
It’s the same word used for Noah’s ark.
Not a coincidence.
Because when God saves, He builds arks.
Little vessels of mercy that float in the middle of judgment.
Imagine the scene.

The early morning mist rising from the Nile.
The quiet movement of reeds along the riverbank.
A mother kneeling in the mud with tears streaming down her face.

Inside the basket…
a sleeping baby.
She knew what that river was known for.

It swallowed lives.
It carried crocodiles.
It had already taken countless Hebrew boys.
And still… she placed her son into the current.
Not because she gave up.
But because she trusted God more than she trusted her own strength.
That basket was not abandonment.
It was surrender.
And what happened next is one of the most shocking reversals in the Bible.

The basket drifted…
right into the world of Pharaoh himself.

Pharaoh’s daughter came to bathe in the river.
She saw the basket among the reeds.
She opened it.
And the baby cried.
That cry changed history.
The princess looked at the child and felt compassion.

The very household that ordered Hebrew babies to die…
would now raise one.
Pharaoh’s palace became the training ground of the future deliverer.
And here’s the detail that almost feels too beautiful to be true.
The princess needed someone to nurse the baby.
So Moses’ sister stepped forward and asked if she should find a Hebrew woman.
Guess who came.
His own mother.
God didn’t just save Moses.

He allowed the woman who surrendered him to raise him…
while Pharaoh’s household paid the wages.
Only God writes stories like that.

The enemy planned genocide.
God prepared a deliverer.
The river meant for death became the road of rescue.
But this story is not just about Moses.
It whispers forward.
Centuries later another child would be born into danger.

A jealous ruler would again order children killed.
Families would again run in fear.
But this child would grow up to do what Moses never could.
His name is Jesus.
Moses would one day lead Israel through the waters of the Red Sea.
But Jesus would step into a deeper river.

The waters of judgment.
The weight of our sin.
The wrath our rebellion deserved.
On the cross, Christ entered the flood for us.
And three days later…
He rose.

The grave could not hold Him.
Death could not silence Him.
The enemy could not stop the rescue plan of God.
That means something powerful for you today.
Maybe you feel like you are standing at the edge of a river.
Something you love feels out of your control.

A dream.
A child.
A future.
A calling.

You’ve prayed.
You’ve fought.
You’ve held on as long as you could.
And now the current looks terrifying.
Listen carefully.
God still rules the river.
The waters that scare you are not stronger than His sovereignty.
The place that feels like loss may actually be the beginning of deliverance.
The basket may feel fragile.
But when something is placed in God’s hands, fragile becomes unstoppable.
Maybe today your step of faith looks like Jochebed’s.
Letting go.
Trusting.
Believing that the God who watches the rivers also watches you.
And if you have never trusted Jesus Christ before, this story is an invitation.
Because the greater Deliverer has already come.
He entered the waters for you.

He died for your sin.
He rose to give you new life.

Repent.
Turn to Him.
Trust the One who rescues what the world says cannot be saved.
Because the same God who carried Moses through the Nile…
is still carrying people through impossible waters today.
And the story of grace is not finished yet.
Someone standing at the edge of a river today needs to remember this truth.
What looked like abandonment… was actually providence.

📖 “But when she could hide him no longer, she got a papyrus basket for him and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in it and put it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.”
— Exodus 2:3
